title: High-yield direct oxidation of methane to methanol with dioxygen

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a practical, continuous process that converts methane directly into methanol using molecular oxygen, supplied as dioxygen or air: CH4 + ½O2 → CH3OH. Methanol would be recovered at a sufficiently high yield and concentration to make the complete process useful. This would bypass the conventional route in which methane is first converted into synthesis gas and methanol is subsequently synthesized from that intermediate.

Scope definition for CHE-02: methane is the carbon feed and dioxygen is the terminal oxidant. Water, solvents, catalysts and regenerable product-protection or separation media may participate, provided their consumption, regeneration and energy requirements are included in the overall process balance. A batch-only experiment or a process consuming stoichiometric peroxide or oleum would not demonstrate this particular capability. The objective combines reaction chemistry, continuous operation and practical product recovery; a selective catalyst alone would establish only part of it.

significance.text: A successful process would eliminate the need to produce syngas as the intermediate between methane and methanol. Latimer and colleagues describe the conventional route as requiring high temperatures and centralized production. Bypassing that route could substantially change methane valorization if the direct process also delivered competitive recovery, productivity and economics. The 2023 review by Blankenship and colleagues identifies conversion of underutilized methane resources into liquid products as a central motivation.

Conditional implications: economical conversion of biogas, stranded gas or methane otherwise flared could become possible, and some applications might support smaller or milder gas-to-liquid plants. These outcomes do not follow automatically from high methanol yield or continuous operation. They also require adequate reactor productivity, heat management, feed cleanup and deployment economics. Replacing existing methanol production or expanding methanol use in fuels and chemicals would require investment in downstream plants and infrastructure.

Interpretive analogy: the comparison with Haber–Bosch concerns the potentially broad reach of an enabling chemical process, rather than a prediction of equal historical impact. CHE-02 addresses one specified transformation and does not imply an ambient electrochemical factory for every commodity. Its potential importance rests on the value of a practical methane-to-methanol route, without requiring an unsupported estimate of how much methane conventional production burns.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central chemical barrier is making methanol without rapidly oxidizing it further. Methanol has more reactive C–H bonds than methane, so conditions that activate methane can also consume the desired product. Latimer, Kakekhani, Kulkarni and Nørskov's 2018 kinetic model explains a selectivity–conversion trade-off in continuous partial oxidation: increasing methane conversion can reduce the fraction of converted carbon recovered as methanol. High selectivity at very low conversion therefore does not, by itself, establish high methanol yield.

The missing capability is simultaneous performance across several process measures. Blankenship, Artsiusheuski, Sushkevich and van Bokhoven's 2023 review calls for improvements in yield, productivity and product concentration together with product protection. A process must make enough methanol per unit of methane and reactor volume while delivering a stream from which methanol can be recovered economically. Improving a catalyst-normalized rate while leaving conversion or concentration unknown does not resolve this engineering challenge.

Product collection, aqueous conditions and diffusion-limited reaction environments are strategies discussed by Latimer and colleagues. Selective adsorption, product protection and integrated removal could help prevent methanol from remaining exposed to oxidizing conditions. These approaches broaden the task beyond a conventional catalyst search, but the supplied evidence does not establish that any one is mandatory or sufficient. The kinetic model is a constraint within its assumptions, not a universal impossibility theorem covering every electrochemical or integrated reactor design.

The thermodynamic and kinetic questions must remain distinct. The 2018 abstract describes direct oxidation as slightly exothermic, but heat release alone does not establish Gibbs-energy favorability under every operating condition. Likewise, demonstrating a favorable reaction or a selective laboratory pathway does not settle the practical requirements of oxygen supply, product recovery, recycle and sustained operation.

current_state.text: In 2018, Latimer and colleagues reported that a practical direct methane-to-methanol process had not been established despite more than a century of research. That statement describes the historical position at publication. The supplied evidence for this paper is an abstract and bibliographic record rather than the full article; it supports the year, authors, kinetic challenge and proposed strategies, but does not verify the earlier research notes' exact June publication date.

The review published on 21 September 2023 reports substantial barriers to translating methane functionalization into practical processes. Its abstract emphasizes coordinated improvement of yield, productivity and product concentration, together with product protection. The supplied review assessment had access to the subscription preview and complete supplementary information, not the main article. The supplement's stated literature coverage runs from January 2017 to approximately May 2022, so it cannot establish the field's position in November 2026. Its figure images were not inspected, and some extracted equations were garbled; the readable reporting recommendations support requiring conversion, an explicit yield basis and volumetric productivity.

Kim and colleagues' report, published on 4 July 2025 in Nature Catalysis, describes room-temperature electrochemical methane-to-methanol conversion on IrO2 using carbonate as the oxygen source. The abstract reports continuous operation and a maximum methanol production rate of approximately 11.1 mmol per gram of catalyst per hour at 1.50 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode. The supplementary tables report 11,060 μmol per gram of catalyst per hour and 93% methanol selectivity for the flow cell at 25 °C and 1 bar. These are reported experimental component achievements, including continuous operation, but they do not establish the specified dioxygen-fed process.

The evidence for the 2025 result extends beyond an abstract: the retained page identifies the authors, and the supplied review assessed supplementary text and tables. However, the main article and relevant quantitative figure plots were not inspected. The assessed material does not establish high single-pass methanol yield or thousands of hours of stable operation. The supplement also contains process modelling and economic analysis; those calculations must be distinguished from measured plant performance. These access limitations leave particular performance questions open without showing that the reported experimental results are false.

Evidence-bounded synthesis: no supplied source demonstrates the complete combination of dioxygen as terminal oxidant, high methane-based single-pass methanol yield, practical recovery and durable continuous operation. The supplied material does not include an updated literature search establishing the wider field's status through 1 November 2026. Consequently, the complete breakthrough is not demonstrated by this record, while its status across the entire literature at that date remains unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed chemical demonstration: operate a continuous reactor with methane as the carbon feed and dioxygen or air as the terminal oxidant, without another consumed stoichiometric oxidant. Establish the overall reactant balance, including regeneration of any protection or separation media. Report methane conversion, methanol selectivity and methane-based single-pass methanol yield together, supported by a complete carbon balance, alongside volumetric productivity and methanol concentration. These proposed measurements would prevent a high mass-normalized production rate or high selectivity at unknown conversion from being mistaken for completion.
completion_criteria.label: Continuous methane oxidation using dioxygen with complete methanol production accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: show stable operation for thousands of hours with credible product recovery at the measured concentration, then publish an integrated material, energy and economic comparison against a clearly defined syngas-route baseline. Include oxygen or air handling, separation, recycle, catalyst replacement, solvent and media losses, and regeneration demands. The measured yield should be high enough for the complete process to outperform that baseline on energy and cost. Distillation or membrane recovery could qualify if justified by the actual stream and process balance. Thousands of hours and comparative economic performance are proposed criteria, not established consensus thresholds; no universal numerical yield target is asserted.
completion_criteria.label: Thousands of stable operating hours beating syngas-route energy and cost

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary demonstration: make methods, balances and operating data sufficiently complete for independent replication, and reproduce the key performance over repeated runs and catalyst preparations. State the demonstrated ranges of feed composition, throughput, temperature, pressure and operating duration, including sensitivity to relevant feed impurities. Testing representative natural-gas or biogas feeds would strengthen claims about those applications. Finite testing would establish breadth within the tested conditions, not universal suitability for every methane source or reactor scale.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible performance across runs and catalyst preparations within stated limits

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison—CHE-01, Ambient nitrogen fixation at industrial rate, efficiency, and lifetime: both concepts seek a practically competitive alternative to an established chemical production route and require simultaneous evidence of rate, efficiency and lifetime. Their chemical objectives remain distinct: nitrogen fixation produces nitrogen compounds, whereas CHE-02 selectively oxidizes methane with dioxygen. CHE-01's ambient-condition objective is not an automatic requirement of CHE-02.

Roster comparison—CHE-03, Fossil-parity olefins and liquid fuels from carbon dioxide, and CHE-06, Direct solar manufacture of fuels and chemicals: these concepts overlap in the possibility of supplying fuels or chemical feedstocks through alternative processes. CHE-02 begins with methane and specifies dioxygen as terminal oxidant; CHE-03 begins with carbon dioxide and requires competitive conversion to different product classes, while CHE-06 specifies direct solar energy use. An electrochemical or solar-assisted methane process could overlap operationally, but it would still need to establish CHE-02's overall reactant balance and performance.

Roster comparison—CHE-04, Plant-scale molecular separations that can retire the hardest distillations: selective methanol removal and recovery could be enabling components of CHE-02. The overlap concerns separation integrated with reaction, including product protection. CHE-04 addresses a broader separation capability; CHE-02 retains its particular methane-to-methanol chemistry. Multifunctional reactor design is a relevant engineering approach, but the supplied evidence does not establish the earlier assertion about its commercial history.

Roster comparison—CHE-05, First-time-right scale-up of multiphase reactors: translating a methane oxidation experiment into sustained production may require control of phase contact, transport and heat removal. Predictive scale-up could help preserve selectivity and productivity at larger throughput. CHE-05 concerns a general scale-up capability, whereas CHE-02 requires successful performance for one specified transformation; neither capability alone demonstrates the other.

Roster comparison—CHE-07, Closed-loop monomers from real mixed plastic waste, CHE-08, Land-free staple calories from carbon dioxide and renewable energy, and CHE-09, Direct air capture near the thermodynamic limit, at climate scale: all require integrated process evidence beyond a favorable isolated reaction or component metric. Their feedstocks and products remain distinct from CHE-02. Methanol production from methane does not itself demonstrate plastic circularity, food manufacture from carbon dioxide, atmospheric carbon capture or a net climate benefit.

Roster comparison—CHE-10, On-demand manufacturing of arbitrary small molecules: methanol could serve as an input to downstream synthesis, but producing one useful platform chemical does not demonstrate arbitrary molecular manufacturing. CHE-02 is a narrowly defined transformation with potentially broad applications; CHE-10 seeks breadth across molecular products and would require separate evidence of synthesis scope.

change_log.change: Preserved CHE-02's identity while clarifying methane as carbon feed and dioxygen or air as terminal oxidant, with regenerable auxiliaries permitted.
change_log.reason: The original wording about using only methane and dioxygen could inadvertently exclude water, solvents and product-protection strategies compatible with the intended overall chemistry.

change_log.change: Replaced the blanket thermodynamic assertion with the supported description of slight exothermicity and distinguished it from condition-dependent Gibbs-energy favorability.
change_log.reason: Exothermicity alone does not establish thermodynamic favorability under unspecified operating conditions.

change_log.change: Retained the selectivity–conversion mechanism and integrated documented collection, aqueous and diffusion-limited strategies without making product removal mandatory.
change_log.reason: The kinetic model supports a design constraint within its assumptions, rather than a universal impossibility theorem or proof of a unique solution.

change_log.change: Corrected the 2025 evidence description to identify Kim and colleagues, credit continuous operation and include supplementary flow-cell performance.
change_log.reason: The retained page contains authors, and the reviewed supplementary tables support 11,060 μmol gcat−1 h−1, 93% selectivity, 25 °C and 1 bar, contradicting the earlier abstract-only description.

change_log.change: Distinguished accessible supplementary information from unavailable main articles and preserved figure and extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: Complete supplementary documents do not constitute access to the main articles or inspection of their quantitative figure plots.

change_log.change: Recast the present-day conclusion as a limitation of the supplied evidence rather than a literature-wide claim of nonachievement.
change_log.reason: The supplied freshness record is empty, so the historical sources and 2025 report cannot establish the entire field's status through 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Made smaller plants, milder operation and use of dispersed methane conditional; retained the Haber–Bosch comparison as an interpretive analogy.
change_log.reason: Those applications require additional engineering and economic performance, and the sources do not support the claim that conventional production burns most of the methane molecule.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include complete balances, volumetric productivity, recovery, defined economic boundaries and independent reproducibility.
change_log.reason: These make the proposed demonstration assessable without presenting candidate-defined yield, durability or economic targets as established standards.

change_log.change: Added explicit distinctions across the supplied concept roster and removed the unsupported commercial-history assertion for multifunctional reactors.
change_log.reason: Engineering overlap should inform CHE-02 without merging concepts or preserving an unverified historical claim.

unresolved_issues: The complete capability's status across the literature through 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because no updated, bounded search record was supplied.

The reviewed 2025 abstract and supplementary text do not establish high methane-based single-pass methanol yield or thousands of hours of stability; uninspected figures or the main article may contain additional relevant evidence.
The 2025 carbonate-fed electrochemical route's complete reactant and regeneration balance would need assessment before any claim that it satisfies a dioxygen-terminal-oxidant process.

It remains open which catalyst and reactor architecture can jointly deliver adequate yield, productivity, concentration, recovery and durability; product protection is a documented strategy rather than a proven exclusive solution.
No authoritative numerical yield or durability threshold is established here. A competitive demonstration requires a defined syngas baseline and explicit deployment assumptions.
The supplied evidence does not resolve the commercial history of multifunctional reactors or verify the earlier exact June 2018 publication date; neither assertion is retained as an established fact.

brief.title: Turning methane directly into liquid methanol
possible: Gas that is now flared or left unused could become methanol, a liquid used in fuels and chemicals. Plants would convert methane gas directly into methanol using oxygen or air, running continuously and recovering enough usable product to make the process worthwhile.
why: Methanol production would skip synthesis gas, the intermediate mixture used in today's route. That would remove a stage that requires high temperatures and centralized production, opening a path to smaller plants serving otherwise underused methane sources.

sources.who: Allegra A. Latimer, Arvin Kakekhani, Ambarish R. Kulkarni and Jens K. Nørskov
sources.showed: Their model explained why reacting more methane can reduce the share that becomes methanol: the desired product reacts more readily than methane does.
sources.quote: Herein, we present a simple kinetic model to explain the selectivity-conversion trade-off that hampers continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol.
sources.cited_for: The model explains the central obstacle to obtaining a high methanol yield during continuous production.
sources.not_established: The model does not establish a practical process or rule out every possible reactor design.

sources.showed: Their review identified the need to improve together the amount of methane becoming useful product, production speed and product concentration, while protecting methanol from further reaction.
sources.cited_for: Success requires the reaction and product recovery to work well together.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a continuous oxygen-fed process that combines these requirements.

sources.showed: They reported that 93% of converted methane became methanol in a continuously operated, electrically driven reactor at room temperature.

as an oxygen source enables efficient and selective electrochemical methane-to-methanol conversion at room temperature.
sources.cited_for: The experiments demonstrate continuous production with a high share of converted methane becoming methanol.
sources.not_established: They do not establish high yield from the methane fed, economical recovery or durable operation using oxygen or air.

shown: Cheolho Kim and colleagues demonstrated a continuous route powered by electricity. It obtains oxygen from carbonate, an oxygen-containing compound. This is a partial achievement toward a process supplied with oxygen or air.
missing: A continuous oxygen-fed process must turn a large enough share of incoming methane into methanol without rapidly consuming the product.
The process must produce methanol fast enough and concentrated enough for economical recovery.
Sustained operation must beat the conventional route on total energy use and cost, including recycling and regeneration.
Independent teams must reproduce the performance across repeated runs and separately prepared reaction materials.

milestones.label: Continuous production with oxygen and complete material accounting
milestones.explanation: A continuous reactor would have to use methane and oxygen or air, account for all inputs and products, and measure yield, production rate and concentration. This would establish how much usable methanol the whole process makes.

milestones.label: Thousands of stable hours with lower energy and cost
milestones.explanation: Operation would have to remain stable for thousands of hours, with measured recovery and a complete comparison showing lower energy use and cost than the conventional route. This would establish practical competitiveness.

milestones.label: Reproducible performance within clearly tested operating limits
milestones.explanation: Independent replication and repeated runs with separately prepared reaction materials would have to reproduce performance, with operating limits and impurity sensitivity stated. This would establish reliability within tested conditions.

uncertain: It remains open which reaction materials and reactor design can combine high yield, fast production, concentrated product and long life.
No universal yield target is established; competitiveness depends on the conventional process and deployment conditions used for comparison.
Thousands of operating hours is a proposed milestone, rather than an agreed scientific threshold.
